articles.title: Raising our sons
articles.author: none@none.com (Van Nguyen)
articles.rss_summary: IN June, a seven-year-old girl in Sargodha went to a grocery store and never returned. In August, an 18-month-old in Karachi lost her life after being sexually assaulted by a teenage relative. Two weeks later, Hina Javed, a 45-year-old professional, was found raped and murdered in her own home in Rawalpindi. Days later, a five-year-old girl in Haripur who had gone out to play was found dead in a well. These cases broke through in a single summer; many more never did. Each time, Pakistan said “never again,” then turned the page. On paper, Pakistan has made progress. The Anti-Rape Act of 2021 and the rules that followed strengthened how rape is investigated and tried, and how survivors are protected. Yet law ministry figures, reported by Dawn, record 47,452 cases across five categories of rape-related offences in the four provinces between 2021 and mid-2026. And that is only the reported picture: the Senate Functional Committee on Human Rights noted that an estimated 70 per cent of gender-based violence incidents go unreported. articles.title: Justice or just this?
articles.author: none@none.com (Mahir Ali)
articles.rss_summary: THE wheels of international justice tend to grind slowly. The Gambia launched its complaint against Myanmar at The Hague in November 2019. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered its verdict last Thursday, seven years later. Following the unprecedented finding that the state was indeed guilty of genocide against the Rohingya minority, the biggest question now is whether it will make much difference to the survivors, most of whom found refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh. Hundreds of thousands more are scattered across various other countries including India and Pakistan, but mostly concentrated in Thailand and Malaysia. The latter, which last month welcomed U Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar’s president and former military chief, regularly threatens deportation. The visiting leader offered to take back all citizens; however, a 1982 law stripped most Rohingya of citizenship. The community’s roots in northern Rakhine state go back centuries, yet politicians, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have long tended to pejoratively (and inaccurately) refer to them as ‘Bengalis’. articles.title: Cashless divide
articles.author: none@none.com (Salma Khan)
articles.rss_summary: IMAGINE a woman in Islamabad arriving at a government office to pay a fee. She has the money, but no bank account and no smartphone of her own. The counter no longer accepts cash. The official points her towards a QR code. She asks someone nearby to make the payment for her. The payment goes through, but she has had to depend on a stranger to make it. This is a hypothetical situation, but it captures a problem beneath the government’s plan to make Islamabad cashless by the end of December. Do people have the means to participate? And what happens to those who do not? There are good reasons to encourage digital payments. They can make transactions easier to trace, reduce delays and help bring economic activity into the formal system. Raast and other payment infrastructure can make this possible at a scale that cash cannot. But encouraging digital payments is different from withdrawing cash before people have a workable alternative. That distinction matters. The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics’ Household Integrated Economic Survey 2024-25 puts the gap in perspective. Internet use among individuals stands at 57 per cent, falling to 49pc in rural areas, compared with 69pc in urban areas.

articles.title: The missing link
articles.author: none@none.com (Dr Niaz Murtaza)
articles.rss_summary: RULERS who don’t bring power closer to people via strong local bodies want us to believe that they will now bring power closer to people via more provinces. So, the false idea of making many provinces as a cure for our many ills is back with a bang. Months after it first emerged , the bang is still more noise than a clarion call of reason. I have seen three key reports against it, but none in its favour. Support — strong on rhetoric but weak on evidence — comes mainly from ministers and friendly analysts. One minister cites Afghanistan’s 34 units. That’s odd as Afghanistan helps us avoid the blushes of being last in South Asia on key governance metrics. It’s a unitary state whose units lack legislative powers and elected bodies. We have 150-plus stronger units (districts) which have elected bodies, at least as per the law. Some cite unitary France’s 18 units. They too lack legislative powers. Counting them is easier than proving they cause its progress. It has democracy and civilian sway, unlike us. articles.title: Absenteeism woes
articles.author: none@none.com (Parvez Rahim)
articles.rss_summary: EMPLOYERS face multiple challenges while managing their businesses. Besides setting up the necessary infrastructure, the quality of manpower plays a key role in the success of an enterprise. The top operating companies in Pakistan, the numbers of which have shrunk substantially over the last 30 to 40 years, employed the best technicians and operators, who were much wanted by petroleum giants, such as Safco and Aramco. Such workers are mostly committed to their company’s interests in complying with safety policies and fulfilling job responsibilities. Regular attendance plays a crucial role in judging an employee’s commitment to his job and organisation. In progressive companies, there is a provision of two weekly rest days, and between 20 to 25 days of annual leave against the statutory requirement of 14 days per annum. The quantum of other leaves in the law comprises 10 days of casual leave, 16 days of sick leave, and around 15 days of festival-related holidays per year. The total number of leaves and holidays is approximately 165 days, leaving just 200 days of work in a year. articles.title: AMR awareness
articles.author: none@none.com (Editorial)
articles.rss_summary: IT is an irony in the world of medicine that even as new treatments bring hope to millions of patients, some older therapies are rapidly losing their efficacy. This point merits serious reflection as we approach the end of World AMR Awareness Week 2026. Although primarily focused on the misuse of antibiotics, which kill bacteria, antimicrobial resistance also encompasses the immunity developed by fungi, viruses, and parasites in the body to standard drugs. The 2026 theme for AMR Awareness Week — ‘One health, one action: prevent AMR now’ — widens the scope of the campaign by underlining the importance of collective efforts and shared responsibility in fighting a scourge that kills millions every year. An interconnected world — where the health of people, animals, and the environment is inextricably linked — demands as much. The numbers are concerning. WHO says that over 4.7m annual deaths worldwide are associated with antibiotic resistance. The number of such deaths is projected to rise to 39m by 2050, with developing countries bearing the brunt. articles.title: Drilling for oil
articles.author: none@none.com (Editorial)
articles.rss_summary: PAKISTAN’S renewed effort to explore oil and gas reserves in its offshore waters, this time in partnership with Turkiye, calls for cautious optimism. We have been here before. Successive governments have pursued offshore exploration. But the efforts have produced little. Some 18 exploratory wells have been drilled in offshore waters since independence. None has resulted in a viable discovery. The most prominent recent attempt was the Kekra-1 well in 2019 , when an international consortium spent around $100m. The well was eventually abandoned without finding oil or gas. That episode was particularly instructive because of the political hype surrounding it. The premier at the time publicly raised expectations of a potentially enormous discovery, suggesting that Pakistan might find enough gas to end its dependence on imports. The speculation generated excitement, only to fizzle out when drilling results proved disappointing. Such premature claims do little to help a sector in which exploration is inherently uncertain and commercial discoveries require years of investment and technical work. articles.author: none@none.com (Editorial)

The bill has sparked significant debate and anger both within and outside the House. It stipulates registration, script approvals, screening of the content for obscenity or defamatory and inflammatory material, and requires organisers to seek permission 15 days prior to holding events and performances. The provincial minister for information and culture defended it as an attempt to regulate, not ban, these performances as well as make them family-friendly. Punjabi theatre, which originates from folk traditions, centralises relatability and familiarity, preferring derision over finesse. Sadly, instead of becoming a unique aspect of the cultural economy, the lack of state patronage has left artists at the mercy of private sponsors and ticket revenues. Since its descent into bawdiness did not happen overnight, an overhaul ought to be gradual and empathetic. articles.title: Rohingya genocide
articles.author: none@none.com (Editorial)
articles.rss_summary: NEARLY a decade after the world watched Myanmar’s junta conduct a brutal campaign of extermination and displacement against the Muslim Rohingya minority, the International Court of Justice has ruled that the regime is guilty of genocide. It took a small African state — The Gambia — to lodge a case at the ICJ against Myanmar. Today, because of The Gambia’s courage and moral clarity, this verdict has made history as it is the first time a state has been held guilty of genocide. While calling out a blood-soaked campaign for what it was, the ruling also sets a legal precedent for building a strong case against another genocidal state: Israel. To recall, in 2017 the Myanmar military unleashed massive violence against the Rohingya in Rakhine state, with thousands killed, including over 2,000 children under five, rampant sexual attacks, while hundreds of thousands of Rohingya were forced to flee. The Rohingya have long faced discrimination, with the regime denying most citizenship. The junta claims it had conducted ‘counterinsurgency operations’, a defence rejected by the ICJ. articles.title: Helping create paths
articles.author: none@none.com (Faisal Bari)
articles.rss_summary: ONE child, born in an affluent household, goes to one of the best private, high-fee schools, gets a lot of support from home, appears for international school leaving assessments and then makes her way to the best colleges and universities of the country or of the world. When she enters the job market, she not only has her education to bank on, and the confidence that comes with it and the upbringing she got, she has parental and university networks to support her as well. Another child — and there are millions of children in Pakistan who face these odds — might have struggled to even be in a public or low-fee private school, is likely to drop out well before reaching college, but even if she reaches college, it is likely she will struggle to find a job afterwards. The quality of her education is compromised, she did not have much support from home for her learning, her confidence has not been built up, and she does not have a parental/family network or a university network to support her. Titled Judicial Capture: Independence of the Judiciary in Pakistan after the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments, the report concludes that systemic constitutional and legislative changes have placed the country’s highest courts under the control of the political and executive branches. The ICJ comprises judges and lawyers from around the world working to “develop and strengthen national and international justice systems”. The report clarifies: “The ICJ does not take a position on the merits of political disputes between the parties. articles.title: Settling disputes
articles.author: none@none.com (Editorial)
articles.rss_summary: WITH almost 2m court cases clogging the lower judiciary — most of them in Punjab — Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s nod to a proposed panchayat system to resolve local-level disputes is expected to be well received by many litigants. Several factors are responsible for a situation in which disputing parties often find themselves waiting for decades before their cases are settled. A shortage of judges, unclear rules, frequent court adjournments, and corruption at all tiers are just a few of the underlying causes. It is no wonder then that informal forums of ‘justice’, based more on centuries-old, often barbaric customs than on modern legal principles, persist in the country. Seen in this light, a panchayat system that prioritises community decision-making but with some state regulation, appears, at least theoretically, to be the right move. However, as with any initiative, it is important to closely study similar local justice schemes elsewhere before embarking on the proposed project. articles.title: Childhoods forsaken
articles.author: none@none.com (Editorial)
articles.rss_summary: WORLD Children’s Day, observed today, should be a celebration of childhood. In Pakistan, it is a reminder of how often children are denied even basic safety. At least 28 schoolchildren died when a roof collapsed in Peshawar last month; in August, a fire at Islamabad’s Pims hospital killed 14 newborns. Both tragedies raise serious questions about safety standards in schools and hospitals. Reports of children raped and murdered, sometimes by people they knew, point to dangers closer to home. Sahil documented 1,914 child abuse cases in the first half of 2026, including 1,015 cases of sexual abuse and 558 abductions. These were only cases reported in newspapers; the true scale of abuse is likely far greater. Children also face exploitation online. A Unicef-backed study estimated that 1.5m internet-using children aged 12 to 17 experienced technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse in a year. Yet despite the scale of these dangers, effective protection remains out of reach. Violence and abuse are only part of the hardship confronting Pakistan’s children. articles.title: Islamic education
articles.author: none@none.com (Ghulam Shabbir)
articles.rss_summary: WHERE the Judeo-Christian tradition — despite its long coexistence with and exposure to Hellenism — failed at the fusion of religious and pure intellectual streams of thought, Islam sutured the fabric of transcendental and empirical reality so seamlessly that it gushed forth to spread like a prairie fire from Baghdad to India, Transoxiana and further still. The Quran so vigorously fired the imagination of Muslims and implanted philosophic spirit in them that within a short time they mastered the sciences and were at the helm of world affairs. However, orthodox elements blew this fusion of metaphysical and social reality into shreds and after a few centuries, the real ‘dark ages’ of Muslims set in. The clergy was left with little more than a threadbare formal structure of ideas. How did things come to such a pass? It was a protracted war between orthodox elements and philosophers, fought from rigid positions which shaped the content of Islamic education and Muslim attitude towards philosophy and positive sciences, of which both Muslim thought and philosophy paid the price.
